title: The silk-cotton tree
hook: the silk-cotton tree is tall and straight, but its fruit is tasteless and its leaves useless (Asa di Var, ang 470)

segments.voice: Yesterday, mitthat neevee, and your line: sweet and humble. How did your sweeter sentence land? Today we go back to the start of that same salok, where Guru Nanak points at a tree. Day five hundred fifty-two.

In parts of North India and Punjab, there's a tree that's hard to miss when it blooms. Its branches are bare, and then suddenly they're covered in huge red flowers, so bright they look painted on. It stands tall and straight, often taller than everything around it. In Punjabi it's the simmal. In English it's called the silk-cotton tree, for the fluffy cotton in its pods. People in Guru Nanak's world knew it well. And he used it to open the salok we met yesterday, as a picture of a certain kind of life.
screen: `RED FLOWERS ON BARE BRANCHES.` → `TALL AND STRAIGHT.` → `THE SIMMAL TREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok's opening on ang 470, in paraphrase. The simmal tree is straight as an arrow, very tall and very thick. But the birds that come to it full of hope go away disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers sickly, and its leaves are of no use. That's the whole picture, and it's sharp. From a distance, the tree has everything: height, straightness, a trunk you can't get your arms around, a blaze of color. A bird flying over would think, there's my meal, there's my shade. It lands, and finds nothing to eat, no shade worth sitting in, nothing that feeds. The tree isn't wicked. It just isn't useful. And then, right after the tree, come the lines we heard yesterday: mitthat neevee are the essence of virtue; the side of the scale that bends low is the heavy one. So the tree is the opposite of the scale. It's all height and no weight. All show and no fruit. The salok keeps going, too. It describes the guilty one who bows twice as low, the way a hunter crouches to stalk a deer. Low, but not humble. And then it asks: what's the use of bowing the head if the heart stays impure? Put together, the lesson is about what people come to us for. Someone in trouble doesn't need us to be impressive. They need fruit: a meal, a kind word, real shade. The salok measures a life by what it gives, not how tall it stands.
screen: `TALL, STRAIGHT, THICK, BRIGHT.` · `THE BIRDS LEAVE DISAPPOINTED.` · `ALL HEIGHT, NO WEIGHT.` · `PEOPLE NEED FRUIT, NOT HEIGHT.` · then, large: `USEFUL, NOT TALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be useful, not just tall. Sit and breathe. Picture the people who might come to you this week, hoping for something: a coworker, a child, a friend, a neighbor. For each one, ask what fruit they'd actually need. Not a performance, not advice to look clever, but something that feeds: time, help, a listening ear. Choose one small fruit you can give today. Hold that picture for a few breaths. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Simmal, the silk-cotton tree: tall, straight and bright, but the birds that come to it in hope leave with nothing.
Your line: useful, not tall. Today, give your one fruit to the person you pictured, and don't mention it on any feed. Day five hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear the salok of the simmal tree in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and teachers use it to describe a life that looks impressive but gives nothing.

match.prompt: the tree and the scale — tap the pairs.
pairs: bows low, but not in humility

myth: in the salok, the simmal tree is short and crooked
it is straight, very tall and very thick, and still gives nothing.
the tree opens the same salok as sweetness and humility
the tree comes first, then mitthat neevee and the scale.
the salok praises anyone who bows low
it pictures a hunter bowing to stalk a deer, and asks what bowing is worth with an impure heart.

fork.setup: you're a bird, tired and hungry, and you see the tallest, brightest tree around. what happens when you land?
options: you find sweet fruit and deep shade.
you find nothing to eat and leave disappointed.
the tree is too tall to reach.
fork.reveal: the birds come to the simmal full of hope and go away disappointed: its fruit is tasteless and its leaves useless.

original.note: Gurmukhi: simmal, the silk-cotton tree, tall and red-flowered, common across Punjab.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty tree in an old poem.
what it means: a life that looks tall and impressive but gives nothing to those who come in hope.
what a scholar hears: the simmal opens the same salok as mitthat neevee; tree and scale are a pair, all height set against true weight.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (simmal rukh saraaiaa), Ang 470

notes: The salok is paraphrased; confirm the tree description (saraaiaa, ati deeragh, ati much), birds coming in hope and leaving disappointed, fruit tasteless (phikke), flowers sickly (bakbake), leaves useless.
The hunter line ('apraadhee doonaa nivai jo hantaa miragaahi') rendered as a hunter crouching to stalk a deer; confirm.
Botany: the simmal (Bombax ceiba, red silk-cotton) flowers on bare branches in late winter to early spring; confirm phrasing.

Fresh review: hook's seasonal claim softened and 'something we've all met... in ourselves' cut; the hunter line now names the guilty one (apraadhee) as the salok does; the closing claim narrowed from Sikh teaching as a whole to the salok. Day 551 no longer teaches the bowing warning, so it is fresh here.
